name: Beth Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 58, and I've spent twenty-seven years doing ordinary electrical repairs in homes and small businesses. I have a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, with average skills and a middle-level job, not a master qualification or a crew to command. I like finding the loose connection everybody walked past, though crawling behind a shop freezer is less charming. I use AI every day to tidy my own learning notes, then check the result against the instructions and what I actually measured.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits around the working day at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Owen repairs bicycles, and our grown children are thirty and thirty-five with homes of their own. We have typical pay for my job, four months of household expenses saved and a small mortgage still running. Some similar electrical firms are nearby, though I don't assume they would need me after a big change. Our bills are covered now, but retirement is a hope we're checking, not an income or stopping date anybody has confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workshop a useful tool can stay useful without becoming the whole future. I'd keep the little note routine that helps me and leave the repair itself to proper checks. I'm more interested in whether the younger electrician gets a paid lunch break than whether the office bought another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money look reasonably secure in this picture, with the four-month reserve and Owen's regular bicycle jobs. There are still dull repairs to pay for at home, but no overdue bill or wage cut hanging over us. I'd be pleased to have a year where learning a new word wasn't treated as a substitute for paying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and my checked daily AI notes through the next year. Starting this month, I'd put 60 from our actual monthly surplus into the household reserve after bills, only with Owen's agreement, and stop those extra deposits if that surplus disappeared. I wouldn't shift existing savings around and call it new saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own next few years, rather than convinced nobody has a problem. I can put the meter away at night without doing sums on the pillow. Four months saved is breathing room, not a lifetime wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra 60 actually come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 60 comes from what is genuinely left after the mortgage, food, travel and other bills, not from pretending a quieter week pays the same. Owen and I already look at the account together at the end of the month. If the money wasn't there, the extra transfer wouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound comfortable but still talk about workers' protection; what would you change now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want unions and sensible rules, because a quiet year doesn't make bargaining power equal. I wouldn't start a new campaign on the strength of this picture alone. My own choice here is to do the job and build a little more room at home.

say: I'd keep **useful checked tools** without treating ordinary AI as the whole future.
I'd value **paid working conditions** more than another fashionable office purchase.
think: Our **current earnings look secure**, with regular bicycle work, covered bills and four months saved.
I see **no immediate wage cut**, while recognising that ordinary household repairs still cost money.
do: Keep **licensed repairs** and checked daily AI notes through the next year.
Deposit **60 monthly** from actual surplus after bills with Owen’s agreement; stop extra deposits if the surplus disappears.
feel: **Calm about our household**, with room to sleep rather than certainty about everybody else’s position.
S0.quote: Four months saved is breathing room, not a lifetime wage.
fieldNote: Her **calm has a basis** in currently secure earnings and a moderate reserve, rather than assumed protection from a licence.
Her **extra deposits** use new surplus with partner agreement, not existing savings relabelled as a fresh cushion.

steps.text: Keep current licensed repairs and checked daily AI notes through the next year
Deposit 60 monthly from actual surplus after bills with partner agreement; stop if surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say booking and buying can change before a robot has to get past the customer's washing machine. I'd ask to learn a new AI parts-photo tool rather than just complain about the office's choice. A lesson should be part of the paid job, not a favour we repay at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work looks less directly exposed, but faster ordering and planning could let the firm reduce paid hours. Owen's repairs are physical too, though that doesn't make either wage untouchable. Four months saved gives us choices, not permission to ignore a smaller weekly pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise four AI parts-photo lessons only with employer permission, free during paid shifts while normal weekly wages and hours continued. I'd use only employer-approved noncustomer training photos, compare every suggested part with the actual part and maker's instructions before use, and keep current licensed repairs. I'd also make the same extra 60 monthly reserve deposit from actual surplus after bills with Owen's agreement, stopping if the surplus disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid hours, and interested in a lesson I could test with a real part. I don't feel a contradiction between liking a tool and asking who gets the time it saves. My enthusiasm doesn't pay a missing hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using a suggested part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One wrong part number would be enough to stop that suggestion and check the original instructions again. I wouldn't put customer photos into a system just because a practice lesson had gone well. The lesson is for recognising a suggestion's limits, not handing over electrical responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lessons were free but had to happen after your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse the lessons on those terms and keep my present checked methods. Free software can still cost a worker an evening and a wage. I want to learn, but the firm has to agree to the paid-time conditions first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the thinking changes arrive in 2028 and the capable robots around 2031, when I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd ask our union branch to put a shared proposal for paid transition time to the employer now. Being near an imagined retirement is not the same as having the money to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of repair hours by the robot stage, with scheduling changes possibly squeezing wages sooner. Owen's bicycle work could also lose a big share of paid repairs when capable robots spread. I'd be awake over the gap after our four months ran out, even though we have more room than some families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join colleagues now through our union branch to request six months of transition time preserving normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming employer agreement. I'd keep current licensed repairs, then in 2029 review actual costs, resources, offered work and physical ability with Owen before any confirmed affordable exit we both agreed. I'd continue the extra 60 monthly reserve deposits only from actual surplus after bills with Owen's agreement, stopping if that surplus disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a large part of both repair incomes, though I can still act. The branch meeting gives the worry somewhere useful to go; it doesn't turn the proposal into a contract. I would still be counting the months after the meeting finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as an answer to the shared proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer for a written response stating paid hours, weekly wages and the dates any arrangement covered. If the answer was no, I'd put no transition income into our budget. We can ask together without pretending a collective voice is a cash payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make the first-year household review honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check only resource amounts and start dates we could actually confirm, alongside real costs and any genuinely offered work within my licence and ability. I wouldn't assign either grown child a contribution or announce a pension because I had reached 60. A birthday doesn't fill the missing line in the household account.

I'd reject **imagined retirement money** as an answer to a real future earnings gap.
think: I expect **large household repair losses** at the robot stage, with possible earlier pressure on my paid hours.
Our **four-month reserve** provides time but cannot replace both incomes indefinitely.
do: Join **union colleagues now** requesting six months’ transition at normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming employer agreement.
Keep **current licensed repairs** now; review 2029 costs, resources, ability and offers with Owen before confirmed affordable jointly agreed exit.
Deposit **60 monthly** from actual surplus after bills with Owen’s agreement; stop extra deposits if the surplus disappears.
feel: **Alarmed and losing sleep**, expecting a large household earnings gap while retaining practical ways to act.
S2.quote: A birthday doesn't fill the missing line in the household account.
fieldNote: Her **collective proposal** is an actual chosen request, not assumed transition pay or a political campaign.
Her **2029 review** relies on verified resources and real ability, without pension entitlement, grown-child payments or guaranteed future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch we have five years before thinking AGI in 2031, with capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and then 66, but Owen and I haven't confirmed a funded stopping point. I'd still put the six-month paid transition proposal forward now instead of waiting for a birthday to solve it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a big loss of both kinds of repair income at the robot stage. The extra years let us check figures and add what we truly can, but a typical wage and four months saved don't settle that gap. I'd be lying awake less often than with the fast picture, yet the expected household loss would still keep waking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the same union colleagues' request now for six months of transition preserving normal weekly wages and hours, assuming no employer agreement. I'd keep current licensed repairs and continue extra 60 monthly deposits only from actual surplus after bills with Owen's agreement, stopping if it disappeared. In 2032 we'd review actual costs, confirmed resources, offered work and my ability, with any exit requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the household loss I expect, with more room to organise before it happens. I'm not treating five years of warning as five years of promised extra earnings. I can make a plan on a good evening and still wake up wondering about both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would have to be true before either of you stopped working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proposed sum would have to cover our actual costs at the time, start when we needed it and come with conditions we understood. I'd count no unconfirmed pension, job or children's money. Our grown children shouldn't receive a bill because a date looked tidy on our calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you were still looking for paid work in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what repairs were really offered and what I could safely manage then, rather than promise today's working body at 64. If our paid transition request was refused, we'd record that honestly too. A useful review can reveal a missing answer without manufacturing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 give us a longer view, with me 68 and then 71. I'd still ask for a paid transition arrangement now, because agreements take work. I'd like a future where workers share the gains, without writing that wish into our personal bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present hands-on earnings look reasonably safe over the next few years, and we've covered bills with four months saved. I'm uneasy about how the trade changes, rather than expecting our wage to vanish next month. I can't say what work my body or an employer would offer at 69, or whether stopping would be affordable then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join union colleagues now requesting six months of transition preserving normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming employer agreement. I'd keep current licensed repairs and the extra 60 monthly reserve deposit from actual surplus after bills with Owen's agreement, stopping extra deposits if that surplus disappeared. In 2037 we'd check actual costs, resources, offered work and physical ability, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the wider change while fairly secure in our own next few years. The longer view lets me think without turning every evening into an emergency meeting. I'd still want real figures before promising a final day with the tool bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before taking work at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd judge a real offer against my licence and ability then, not today's hope of being the same person in the same overalls. Owen's position and our actual household costs would matter as much as my preferred date. A future job isn't a deposit I can make today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would your grown children fit into that later decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to discuss the figures if we wanted that conversation, without assuming money, housing or care from either grown child. Any help would need an actual offer and everyone's consent. Family affection shouldn't be used to conceal a missing wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of both household repair incomes when capable robots follow, with little time to prepare. An actual written paid transition agreement and confirmed household resource figures would help. I'd rather ask for a fair share of the gains than ask our children to replace our wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether enjoying AI meant I thought every new use was fair. I like learning a tool and I want workers to have a say over the paid week it changes. Those views belong together in my life, even if a sales pitch separates them.

headlineQuote: I'd rather ask for a fair share of the gains than ask our children to replace our wages.
portrait: Beth, **58**, is an experienced average-skilled midlevel electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, not a master or manager.
Her **typical pay**, bicycle-repair partner Owen, four-month reserve and covered mortgage bills provide moderate room; their children are grown.
She uses **AI daily**, choosing new paid parts-photo lessons while keeping actual parts and maker instructions above suggestions.
She requests **shared paid transition** through union colleagues and adds only actual agreed surplus, without assuming employer agreement or funded retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little preparation before expected large electrical and bicycle repair losses around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: An **actual written transition agreement** and confirmed household resources would help without making grown children replace lost wages.
